claim: CFTR is the anion channel mutated in cystic fibrosis patients.
source: CFTR, the anion channel mutated in cystic fibrosis patients, is a model ABC protein whose ATP-driven conformational cycle is observable at single-molecule level in patch-clamp recordings.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CFTR and cystic fibrosis.

claim: CFTR is a model ABC protein whose ATP-driven conformational cycle is observable at single-molecule level in patch-clamp recordings.
source: CFTR, the anion channel mutated in cystic fibrosis patients, is a model ABC protein whose ATP-driven conformational cycle is observable at single-molecule level in patch-clamp recordings.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR's properties as an experimental model system.

claim: Bursts of CFTR pore openings are coupled to tight dimerization of its two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs).
source: Bursts of CFTR pore openings are coupled to tight dimerization of its two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) and in wild-type (WT) channels are mostly terminated by ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited throughout the manuscript and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: In wild-type (WT) CFTR channels, bursts are mostly terminated by ATP hydrolysis.
source: Bursts of CFTR pore openings are coupled to tight dimerization of its two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) and in wild-type (WT) channels are mostly terminated by ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about WT CFTR gating behavior.

claim: The slow rate of non-hydrolytic closure determines how tightly bursts and ATP hydrolysis are coupled.
source: The slow rate of non-hydrolytic closure – which determines how tightly bursts and ATP hydrolysis are coupled – is unknown, as burst durations of catalytic site mutants span a range of ~200-fold.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the kinetic model of CFTR gating.

claim: The slow rate of non-hydrolytic closure is unknown.
source: The slow rate of non-hydrolytic closure – which determines how tightly bursts and ATP hydrolysis are coupled – is unknown, as burst durations of catalytic site mutants span a range of ~200-fold.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: Burst durations of catalytic site mutants span a range of ~200-fold.
source: The slow rate of non-hydrolytic closure – which determines how tightly bursts and ATP hydrolysis are coupled – is unknown, as burst durations of catalytic site mutants span a range of ~200-fold.
evidence: This is supported by data from prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Walker A mutation K1250A completely disrupts ATP hydrolysis.
source: Here, we show that Walker A mutation K1250A, Walker B mutation D1370N, and catalytic glutamate mutations E1371S and E1371Q all completely disrupt ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing no further effect of combining mutations.

claim: Walker B mutation D1370N completely disrupts ATP hydrolysis.
source: Here, we show that Walker A mutation K1250A, Walker B mutation D1370N, and catalytic glutamate mutations E1371S and E1371Q all completely disrupt ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing no further effect of combining mutations.

claim: Catalytic glutamate mutation E1371S completely disrupts ATP hydrolysis.
source: Here, we show that Walker A mutation K1250A, Walker B mutation D1370N, and catalytic glutamate mutations E1371S and E1371Q all completely disrupt ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing no further effect of combining mutations.

claim: Catalytic glutamate mutation E1371Q completely disrupts ATP hydrolysis.
source: Here, we show that Walker A mutation K1250A, Walker B mutation D1370N, and catalytic glutamate mutations E1371S and E1371Q all completely disrupt ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing no further effect of combining mutations.

claim: True non-hydrolytic closing rate of WT CFTR approximates that of K1250A.
source: True non-hydrolytic closing rate of WT CFTR approximates that of K1250A and E1371S.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data showing that these mutations do not alter B1-state stability.

claim: True non-hydrolytic closing rate of WT CFTR approximates that of E1371S.
source: True non-hydrolytic closing rate of WT CFTR approximates that of K1250A and E1371S.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data showing that these mutations do not alter B1-state stability.

claim: The non-hydrolytic closing rate is slowed ~15-fold in E1371Q by a non-native inter-NBD H-bond.
source: That rate is slowed ~15-fold in E1371Q by a non-native inter-NBD H-bond, and accelerated ~15-fold in D1370N.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from macroscopic current relaxations and mutant cycle analysis.

claim: The non-hydrolytic closing rate is accelerated ~15-fold in D1370N.
source: That rate is slowed ~15-fold in E1371Q by a non-native inter-NBD H-bond, and accelerated ~15-fold in D1370N.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from macroscopic current relaxations.

claim: CFTR (ABCC7) is the only known ion channel member of the family of ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) proteins.
source: CFTR (ABCC7) is the only known ion channel member of the family of ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR's unique position in the ABC protein family.

claim: CFTR is a key component of transepithelial salt-water transport in the lung, the pancreas and the intestine.
source: The CFTR anion channel is a key component of transepithelial salt-water transport in the lung, the pancreas and the intestine, and its mutations cause cystic fibrosis (O'Sullivan and Freedman, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Sullivan and Freedman, 2009.

claim: Mutations in CFTR cause cystic fibrosis.
source: The CFTR anion channel is a key component of transepithelial salt-water transport in the lung, the pancreas and the intestine, and its mutations cause cystic fibrosis (O'Sullivan and Freedman, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Sullivan and Freedman, 2009.

claim: CFTR's regulatory (R) region must be phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) to allow channel activity.
source: Its two ABC-typical halfs, each consisting of a transmembrane domain (TMD1 and 2, Figure 1A, gray) followed by a cytosolic nucleotide-binding domain (NBD1 and 2; Figure 1A, blue and green), are linked by a unique regulatory (R) region (Figure 1A, pale red) which must be phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) to allow channel activity (Riordan et al., 1989; Cheng et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Riordan et al., 1989 and Cheng et al., 1991.

claim: ABC proteins are present in all kingdoms of life.
source: ABC proteins are present in all kingdoms of life.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ubiquity of ABC proteins.

claim: The 48 human ABC proteins play essential physiological roles by mediating transmembrane transport of a variety of substrates.
source: The 48 human ABC proteins play essential physiological roles by mediating transmembrane transport of a variety of substrates (Dean et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dean et al., 2022.

claim: Within the ABC family the NBDs are the most highly conserved modules.
source: Within the ABC family the NBDs are the most highly conserved modules, and consist of a core subdomain that binds ATP (the 'head') and an ABC-specific alpha-helical subdomain (the 'tail').
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC protein structure.

claim: NBDs consist of a core subdomain that binds ATP (the 'head') and an ABC-specific alpha-helical subdomain (the 'tail').
source: Within the ABC family the NBDs are the most highly conserved modules, and consist of a core subdomain that binds ATP (the 'head') and an ABC-specific alpha-helical subdomain (the 'tail').
evidence: This is established knowledge about NBD structure.

claim: In all ABC proteins in the presence of ATP the two NBDs form a tight head-to-tail dimer which occludes two ATP molecules at the interface.
source: In all ABC proteins in the presence of ATP the two NBDs form a tight head-to-tail dimer which occludes two ATP molecules (Figure 1B, yellow) at the interface.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC protein structure and function.

claim: The ATP-bound NBD dimer is stable, but is disrupted following ATP hydrolysis.
source: The ATP-bound NBD dimer is stable, but is disrupted following ATP hydrolysis (Locher, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Locher, 2016.

claim: In a subset of ABC proteins, which includes the entire C subfamily, only one of the two composite ATP-binding sites is catalytically active.
source: In a subset of ABC proteins, which includes the entire C subfamily, only one of these two composite ATP-binding sites is catalytically active (Procko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Procko et al., 2009.

claim: In CFTR the composite site formed by the head of NBD2 and the tail of NBD1 ('site 2') contains canonical sequence motifs and hydrolyzes ATP with an overall turnover number of ~0.5–1 s−1.
source: In CFTR the composite site formed by the head of NBD2 and the tail of NBD1 ('site 2', Figure 1B, upper site) contains canonical sequence motifs and hydrolyzes ATP with an overall turnover number of ~0.5–1 s−1 (Li et al., 1996; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 1996 and Liu et al., 2017.

claim: In CFTR, site 1 has accumulated non-canonical substitutions in several key motifs and is catalytically inactive.
source: In contrast, the other site ('site 1', Figure 1B, lower site) has accumulated non-canonical substitutions in several key motifs (Figure 1B, pale residues) and is catalytically inactive (Aleksandrov et al., 2002; Basso et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aleksandrov et al., 2002 and Basso et al., 2003.

claim: During substrate transport the TMDs of ABC exporters alternate between inward-facing (IF) and outward-facing (OF) conformations.
source: During substrate transport the TMDs of ABC exporters alternate between inward-facing (IF) and outward-facing (OF) conformations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC exporter mechanism.

claim: In a phosphorylated CFTR channel opening and closure of the transmembrane ion pore (gating) follows analogous TMD movements.
source: In a phosphorylated CFTR channel opening and closure of the transmembrane ion pore (gating) follows analogous TMD movements (Csanády et al., 2019; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Csanády et al., 2019.

claim: CFTR likely adopts an IF conformation, in which the pore is sealed near its extracellular end, during the long lived (~1 s) state which corresponds to long 'interburst' (IB) closed dwell times observable in single channel current recordings.
source: CFTR likely adopts an IF conformation, in which the pore is sealed near its extracellular end, during the long lived (~1 s) state (Figure 1C, left) which corresponds to long 'interburst' (IB) closed dwell times observable in single channel current recordings.
evidence: This is inferred from structural and functional data.

claim: When CFTR adopts the OF conformation the external gate is predominantly open.
source: When CFTR adopts the OF conformation the external gate is predominantly open, and a lateral portal which connects the channel pore with the cytosol generates a transmembrane aqueous pathway permeable to anions (Zhang et al., 2018; Figure 1C, right, double arrows).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: A lateral portal which connects the channel pore with the cytosol generates a transmembrane aqueous pathway permeable to anions in the OF conformation.
source: When CFTR adopts the OF conformation the external gate is predominantly open, and a lateral portal which connects the channel pore with the cytosol generates a transmembrane aqueous pathway permeable to anions (Zhang et al., 2018; Figure 1C, right, double arrows).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: The continuity of the transmembrane pore is occasionally disrupted for brief (~10 ms) intervals by a smaller conformational change likely confined to the external ends of the TMD helices.
source: However, functional studies show that the continuity of the transmembrane pore is occasionally disrupted for brief (~10 ms) intervals by a smaller conformational change (not depicted in Figure 1C) likely confined to the external ends of the TMD helices (Zhang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Simon and Csanády, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2017, Zhang et al., 2018, and Simon and Csanády, 2021.

claim: In single-channel recordings, the 'OF' or 'bursting' (B) state corresponds to clusters of channel openings separated by brief (flickery) closures.
source: Correspondingly, in single-channel recordings, this 'OF' or 'bursting' (B) state corresponds to clusters of channel openings separated by brief (flickery) closures (Winter et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Winter et al., 1994.

claim: The OF state is relatively stable, with a dwell time of hundreds of milliseconds.
source: The OF state is also relatively stable, with a dwell time of hundreds of milliseconds.
evidence: This is established knowledge from functional studies.

claim: In ABC exporters NBD and TMD movements are coupled: formation of the tight ATP-bound NBD dimer flips the TMDs from an IF to an OF conformation, and disruption of the tight NBD dimer following ATP hydrolysis resets the TMDs to the IF conformation.
source: In ABC exporters NBD and TMD movements are coupled: formation of the tight ATP-bound NBD dimer flips the TMDs from an IF to an OF conformation, and disruption of the tight NBD dimer following ATP hydrolysis resets the TMDs to the IF conformation (Locher, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Locher, 2016.

claim: Gating of phosphorylated CFTR channels is driven by an analogous unidirectional conformational cycle.
source: Gating of phosphorylated CFTR channels is driven by an analogous unidirectional conformational cycle (Csanády et al., 2019; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Csanády et al., 2019.

claim: In all ABCC proteins, the OF state of the TMDs is coupled to tight dimerization of both NBD catalytic sites.
source: In all ABCC proteins, the OF state of the TMDs is coupled to tight dimerization of both NBD catalytic sites (Johnson and Chen, 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson and Chen, 2018, Zhang et al., 2018, and Huang et al., 2023.

claim: Functional studies on CFTR showed that site 2 is tightly dimerized in the B state.
source: Correspondingly, functional studies on CFTR showed that site 2 is tightly dimerized in the B state (Vergani et al., 2005; Figure 1C, right).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vergani et al., 2005.

claim: In IF structures of ABCC proteins obtained in the absence of ATP, or for unphosphorylated CFTR even in its presence, the NBDs are seen to widely separate losing all contact across both composite sites.
source: In contrast, in IF structures of ABCC proteins obtained in the absence of ATP (Johnson and Chen, 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2023), or for unphosphorylated CFTR even in its presence (Levring et al., 2023), the NBDs are seen to widely separate losing all contact across both composite sites.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson and Chen, 2017, Liu et al., 2017, Huang et al., 2023, and Levring et al., 2023.

claim: In the asymmetric bacterial ABC protein Tm287–288 some contacts across the degenerate site are retained throughout the entire conformational cycle, even in the IF state.
source: Interestingly, in the asymmetric bacterial ABC protein Tm287–288 some contacts across the degenerate site are retained throughout the entire conformational cycle, even in the IF state, as shown by extensive structural (Hohl et al., 2012; Hohl et al., 2014) and functional (Timachi et al., 2017) studies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hohl et al., 2012, Hohl et al., 2014, and Timachi et al., 2017.

claim: For phosphorylated CFTR channels functional studies suggested that site 1 does not completely separate throughout the entire ATP-driven gating cycle, even during IB events.
source: Similarly, for phosphorylated CFTR channels functional studies suggested that site 1 does not completely separate throughout the entire ATP-driven gating cycle, even during IB events (Tsai et al., 2010; Szollosi et al., 2011) (see NBDs in Figure 1C, left), a prediction confirmed by recent single-molecule FRET measurements (Levring et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsai et al., 2010, Szollosi et al., 2011, and Levring et al., 2023.

claim: In ABC exporters thermodynamically uphill transport requires unidirectional conformational cycling.
source: In ABC exporters thermodynamically uphill transport requires unidirectional conformational cycling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC exporter mechanism.

claim: The 'coupling ratio' (CR) depends on the relative rates of the two possible exit pathways from the prehydrolytic OF state.
source: The 'coupling ratio' (CR), that is, the fraction of initiated cyles that are completed through ATP hydrolysis, depends on the relative rates of the two possible exit pathways from the prehydrolytic OF state.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the kinetic model.

claim: In CFTR direct measurements of conformational dwell times are made feasible by single-channel current recordings, providing estimates for microscopic transition rates.
source: In most ABC transporters the actual values of these rates are hard to directly estimate, but in CFTR direct measurements of conformational dwell times are made feasible by single-channel current recordings, providing estimates for microscopic transition rates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR as an experimental system.

claim: For a wild-type (WT) channel ATP hydrolysis rate (k1) vs. non-hydrolytic NBD dimer dissociation rate (k−1) can be estimated.
source: Thus, for a wild-type (WT) channel ATP hydrolysis (rate k1, Figure 1C) vs. non-hydrolytic NBD dimer dissociation rate (k−1, Figure 1C) can be estimated.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the experimental approach.

claim: Because k1 >> k−1, CR = k1/(k1 + k−1) is near unity for WT CFTR.
source: Because k1 >> k−1, CR = k1/(k1 + k−1) is near unity.
evidence: This is a mathematical inference from the rate constants.

claim: For WT CFTR the mean burst duration (τb) reports the sum of the life times of the prehydrolytic and posthydrolytic OF conformations.
source: In particular, for WT CFTR the mean burst duration (τb) reports the sum of the life times of the prehydrolytic (Figure 1C, state B1) and posthydrolytic (Figure 1C, state B2) OF conformations.
evidence: This is an inference from the kinetic model.

claim: The life time of B2 is short compared to that of B1 (k2 >> k1).
source: Because the life time of B2 is short compared to that of B1 (k2 >> k1; Figure 1C; Gunderson and Kopito, 1995; Csanády et al., 2010), 1/τb provides a rough estimate of rate k1, which is ~4–5 s−1 at room temperature for pre-phosphorylated CFTR channels gating in ATP.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gunderson and Kopito, 1995 and Csanády et al., 2010.

claim: 1/τb provides a rough estimate of rate k1, which is ~4–5 s−1 at room temperature for pre-phosphorylated CFTR channels gating in ATP.
source: Because the life time of B2 is short compared to that of B1 (k2 >> k1; Figure 1C; Gunderson and Kopito, 1995; Csanády et al., 2010), 1/τb provides a rough estimate of rate k1, which is ~4–5 s−1 at room temperature for pre-phosphorylated CFTR channels gating in ATP.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gunderson and Kopito, 1995 and Csanády et al., 2010.

claim: Rate k−1 in WT CFTR is difficult to directly assess.
source: In contrast, rate k−1 in WT CFTR is difficult to directly assess, and its estimates are based on the burst-state stability of various catalytic site mutants (Figure 1A, red star) in which ATP hydrolysis is disrupted (Figure 1C, red cross) and gating in saturating ATP is thus reduced to reversible IB1 ↔ B1 transitions (Figure 1B, red box).
evidence: This is stated as a challenge motivating the study.

claim: Estimates of k−1 are based on the burst-state stability of various catalytic site mutants in which ATP hydrolysis is disrupted.
source: In contrast, rate k−1 in WT CFTR is difficult to directly assess, and its estimates are based on the burst-state stability of various catalytic site mutants (Figure 1A, red star) in which ATP hydrolysis is disrupted (Figure 1C, red cross) and gating in saturating ATP is thus reduced to reversible IB1 ↔ B1 transitions (Figure 1B, red box).
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for using mutants.

claim: Non-hydrolytic closing rates of various catalytic site mutants scatter over a range of ~200-fold, from ~0.0025 s−1 for E1371Q to ~0.5–1 s−1 for D1370N.
source: However, interpretation of such mutant data is hampered by the fact that – even when compared under identical experimental conditions (expression system, temperature, and phosphorylation state) – non-hydrolytic closing rates of the above mutants scatter over a range of ~200-fold, from ~0.0025 s−1 for E1371Q (Vergani et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2016) to ~0.5–1 s−1 for D1370N (Vergani et al., 2003; Yeh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vergani et al., 2005, Yu et al., 2016, Vergani et al., 2003, and Yeh et al., 2015.

claim: The reason for the large scatter in non-hydrolytic closing rates is unknown.
source: The reason for that large scatter is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: So far all OF structures of CFTR, as well as OF structures of several other ABC proteins, were obtained from E-to-Q catalytic glutamate mutants.
source: Of note, so far all OF structures of CFTR (PDBID: 6msm, 6o2p, 6o1v, 7svd, 7sv7), as well as OF structures of several other ABC proteins (6bhu, 6cov, 6hbu, 6s7p, 7ekl, 8iza), were obtained from E-to-Q catalytic glutamate mutants.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about structural biology practice.

claim: For hCFTR a large difference between the burst durations of the serine vs. glutamine mutant of the catalytic glutamate (hE1371S vs. hE1371Q) had long been documented.
source: Whereas for hCFTR a large difference between the burst durations of the serine vs. glutamine mutant of the catalytic glutamate (hE1371S vs. hE1371Q) had long been documented (cf., Figure 2A, black vs. dark blue trace; Figure 2B, black vs. dark blue symbols), no significant difference (p = 0.092) between τb of the analogous mutants of the zebrafish ortholog (zE1372S vs. zE1372Q; Figure 2A, brown vs. light blue trace; Figure 2B, brown vs. light blue symbols) was detectable (Simon and Csanády, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: No significant difference (p = 0.092) between τb of the analogous mutants of the zebrafish ortholog (zE1372S vs. zE1372Q) was detectable.
source: Whereas for hCFTR a large difference between the burst durations of the serine vs. glutamine mutant of the catalytic glutamate (hE1371S vs. hE1371Q) had long been documented (cf., Figure 2A, black vs. dark blue trace; Figure 2B, black vs. dark blue symbols), no significant difference (p = 0.092) between τb of the analogous mutants of the zebrafish ortholog (zE1372S vs. zE1372Q; Figure 2A, brown vs. light blue trace; Figure 2B, brown vs. light blue symbols) was detectable (Simon and Csanády, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and 2B and citation to Simon and Csanády, 2023.

claim: In hCFTR (PDBID: 6msm) a hydrogen bond is formed between the amide nitrogen of the engineered hQ1371 side chain and the peptide carbonyl oxygen of residue hG576, located in the opposing D-loop of NBD1.
source: In hCFTR (PDBID: 6msm) close examination identified a hydrogen bond across the site 2 interface, formed between the amide nitrogen of the engineered hQ1371 side chain and the peptide carbonyl oxygen of residue hG576, located in the opposing D-loop of NBD1 (Figure 2E, purple dotted line; cf., electron density in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from PDBID: 6msm shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The H-bond between hQ1371 and hG576 cannot be present in WT CFTR, as the native hE1371 side chain contains no chemical moiety suitable to form a stabilizing interaction with the opposing carbonyl group.
source: That H-bond cannot be present in WT CFTR, as the native hE1371 side chain contains no chemical moiety suitable to form a stabilizing interaction with the opposing carbonyl group.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on chemical properties.

claim: In the zCFTR structure (PDBID: 5w81) the amide and carbonyl groups of the zQ1372 side chain are swapped.
source: Interestingly, in the zCFTR structure (PDBID: 5w81) the amide and carbonyl groups of the zQ1372 side chain are swapped.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: The distance between the zQ1372 nitrogen and the backbone carbonyl group of zH576 is substantially larger (4.3 vs. 3.0 Å) than in hCFTR, precluding formation of an H-bond.
source: Thus, although residue hG576 aligns with zT575, the zQ1372 nitrogen points toward the backbone carbonyl group of zH576 and the distance between the two groups is substantially larger (4.3 vs. 3.0 Å), precluding formation of an H-bond (Figure 2F, light purple dotted line).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The >10-fold longer life time of the bursting state of hE1371Q compared to hE1371S CFTR reflects artificial stabilization of state B1 by the introduced non-native interfacial H-bond, which is absent in the zebrafish channel.
source: These observations raised the possibility that the >10-fold longer life time of the bursting state of hE1371Q compared to hE1371S CFTR (Figure 2A, B) reflects artificial stabilization of state B1 by the introduced non-native interfacial H-bond, which is absent in the zebrafish channel.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: In the hE1371Q background deletion of residue hG576 decreased τb by ~20-fold.
source: Whereas in the hE1371Q background deletion of residue hG576 decreased τb by ~20-fold (Figure 3A, orange vs. black trace; Figure 3B, orange vs. black symbols), in the hE1371S background the effect on τb of the same deletion was only ~2-fold (Figure 3A, green vs. blue trace; Figure 3B, green vs. blue symbols).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: In the hE1371S background the effect on τb of hG576 deletion was only ~2-fold.
source: Whereas in the hE1371Q background deletion of residue hG576 decreased τb by ~20-fold (Figure 3A, orange vs. black trace; Figure 3B, orange vs. black symbols), in the hE1371S background the effect on τb of the same deletion was only ~2-fold (Figure 3A, green vs. blue trace; Figure 3B, green vs. blue symbols).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: ΔΔGint(B1 → T‡) is significantly different from zero (p = 4.6 × 10−5).
source: That ΔΔGint(B1 → T‡) is significantly different from zero (p = 4.6 × 10−5), its magnitude (2.3 ± 0.3 kT) is comparable to that of an H-bond, and its positive signature reports that the bond is present in the B1 state, but not in state T‡.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of ΔΔGint(B1 → T‡) (2.3 ± 0.3 kT) is comparable to that of an H-bond.
source: That ΔΔGint(B1 → T‡) is significantly different from zero (p = 4.6 × 10−5), its magnitude (2.3 ± 0.3 kT) is comparable to that of an H-bond, and its positive signature reports that the bond is present in the B1 state, but not in state T‡.
evidence: This is an inference based on known energetics of hydrogen bonds.

claim: The positive signature of ΔΔGint(B1 → T‡) reports that the bond is present in the B1 state, but not in state T‡.
source: That ΔΔGint(B1 → T‡) is significantly different from zero (p = 4.6 × 10−5), its magnitude (2.3 ± 0.3 kT) is comparable to that of an H-bond, and its positive signature reports that the bond is present in the B1 state, but not in state T‡.
evidence: This is an inference from the thermodynamic analysis.

claim: The hG576-hQ1371 H-bond is present selectively in the B state.
source: Because in the IB state separation of the NBD interfaces of site 2 (Vergani et al., 2005) renders formation of the inter-NBD H-bond unlikely, these results suggest that the bond is present selectively in the B state.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and prior knowledge about NBD separation.

claim: The high intraburst Po of the hE1371Q background construct (Po|B = 0.91 ± 0.1 (n = 5)) was not reduced in any of the single or double mutants.
source: In contrast to the large effects of the mutations on τb, the high intraburst Po of the hE1371Q background construct (Po|B = 0.91 ± 0.1 (n = 5)) was not reduced in any of the single or double mutants, for all of which Keq|B values remained within ~twofold (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: An interaction energy ΔΔGint(Cf → O) of 0.44 ±0.36 kT is not significantly different from zero (p = 0.29).
source: Correspondingly, a mutant cycle built on Keq|B (Figure 3F) revealed an interaction energy ΔΔGint(Cf → O) of 0.44 ±0 .36 kT (Figure 3F, purple), which is not significantly different from zero (p = 0.29) suggesting that the strength of the interaction does not change significantly between the flickery closed and the open state.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The strength of the hG576-hQ1371 interaction does not change significantly between the flickery closed and the open state.
source: Correspondingly, a mutant cycle built on Keq|B (Figure 3F) revealed an interaction energy ΔΔGint(Cf → O) of 0.44 ±0 .36 kT (Figure 3F, purple), which is not significantly different from zero (p = 0.29) suggesting that the strength of the interaction does not change significantly between the flickery closed and the open state.
evidence: This is inferred from the thermodynamic analysis.

claim: Deletion of zT575 shortened τb by ~20-fold, whether it was introduced into a zE1372Q or a zE1372S background.
source: Thus, deletion of zT575 shortened τb by ~20-fold, whether it was introduced into a zE1372Q (Figure 4A, orange vs. brown trace; Figure 4B, orange vs. brown symbol) or a zE1372S (Figure 4A, green vs. blue trace; Figure 4B, green vs. blue symbol) background.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The coupling energy calculated from the zT575 deletion mutant cycle, ΔΔGint(B1 → T‡) = 0.34 ± 0.22 kT, is not significantly different from zero (p = 0.17).
source: The coupling energy calculated from the resulting mutant cycle (Figure 4C), ΔΔGint(B1 → T‡) = 0.34 ± 0.22 kT, is not significantly different from zero (p = 0.17).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Deletion of zH576 shortened τb by ~10-fold in the zE1372Q background, and by ~20-fold in the zE1372S background.
source: Similarly, deletion of zH576 shortened τb by ~10-fold in the zE1372Q background (Figure 4D, magenta vs. brown trace; Figure 4E, magenta vs. brown symbol), and by ~20-fold in the zE1372S background (Figure 4D, green vs. blue trace; Figure 4E, green vs. blue symbol), resulting in a calculated coupling energy (Figure 4F) of −0.60 ± 0.28 kT, again not significantly different from zero (p = 0.073).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: The coupling energy from the zH576 deletion mutant cycle of −0.60 ± 0.28 kT is not significantly different from zero (p = 0.073).
source: Similarly, deletion of zH576 shortened τb by ~10-fold in the zE1372Q background (Figure 4D, magenta vs. brown trace; Figure 4E, magenta vs. brown symbol), and by ~20-fold in the zE1372S background (Figure 4D, green vs. blue trace; Figure 4E, green vs. blue symbol), resulting in a calculated coupling energy (Figure 4F) of −0.60 ± 0.28 kT, again not significantly different from zero (p = 0.073).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Introducing the hE1371S mutation into the hK1250A background did not significantly alter τb (p = 0.13).
source: However, introducing the hE1371S mutation into the hK1250A background did not significantly alter τb (p = 0.13) (Figure 5B, blue vs. gray trace, Figure 5C, blue vs. gray symbol).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Mutation hK1250A caused a slight (~28%) but insignificant (p = 0.052) shortening of τb in the hE1371S background.
source: When viewed from a different angle, mutation hK1250A also fails to prolong τb in the hE1371S background (Figure 5B, C, blue vs. Figure 3A, B, blue); instead it caused a slight (~28%) but insignificant (p = 0.052) shortening.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B, 5C, and Figure 3A, 3B.

claim: ATP hydrolysis is already completely abolished in both hK1250A and hE1371S single mutants.
source: These results together indicate that ATP hydrolysis is already completely abolished in both single mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effects of combining the mutations.

claim: Introducing the hE1371S mutation into the hD1370N background did not significantly alter τb (p = 0.09).
source: However, introducing the hE1371S mutation into the hD1370N background did not significantly alter τb (p = 0.09) (Figure 5D, blue vs. gray trace, Figure 5E, blue vs. gray symbol), suggesting complete lack of ATP hydrolysis in the hD1370N single mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: There is complete lack of ATP hydrolysis in the hD1370N single mutant.
source: However, introducing the hE1371S mutation into the hD1370N background did not significantly alter τb (p = 0.09) (Figure 5D, blue vs. gray trace, Figure 5E, blue vs. gray symbol), suggesting complete lack of ATP hydrolysis in the hD1370N single mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of adding the hE1371S mutation.

claim: Introducing mutation hE1371Q into an hK1250A background further increased τb by ~fivefold (p = 2.4 × 10−5) indicating strong stabilization of state B1 by the hE1371Q mutation.
source: Indeed, introducing mutation hE1371Q into an hK1250A background further increased τb by ~fivefold (p = 2.4 × 10−5) indicating strong stabilization of state B1 by the hE1371Q mutation (Figure 5B, black vs. gray trace, Figure 5C, black vs. gray symbol).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Introducing the hE1371Q mutation into an hD1370N background further increased τb by ~16-fold (p = 1.7 × 10−4), indicating strong stabilization of the B1 state.
source: Similarly, introducing the hE1371Q mutation into an hD1370N background further increased τb by ~16-fold (p = 1.7 × 10−4), again indicating strong stabilization of the B1 state (Figure 5D, black vs. gray trace, Figure 5E, black vs. gray symbol).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: In ABC proteins the E-to-Q mutation of the catalytic base abrogates ATP hydrolysis and traps isolated NBD proteins in stable dimer form.
source: In ABC proteins the E-to-Q mutation of the catalytic base, a conserved glutamate that follows the Walker B aspartate, abrogates ATP hydrolysis and traps isolated NBD proteins in stable dimer form (Moody et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2002; Janas et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moody et al., 2002, Smith et al., 2002, and Janas et al., 2003.

claim: E-to-Q mutants have been adopted as model systems in a multitude of structural studies, in an attempt to trap the protein in a prehydrolytic state.
source: For that reason, E-to-Q mutants have been adopted as model systems in a multitude of structural studies, in an attempt to trap the protein in a prehydrolytic state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about structural biology practice.

claim: Under cryo-EM conditions in the presence of ATP full-length E-to-Q mutant ABC proteins yield OF structures in which ATP is seen intact, confirming lack of hydrolysis.
source: Indeed, under cryo-EM conditions in the presence of ATP full-length E-to-Q mutant ABC proteins yield OF structures in which ATP is seen intact, confirming lack of hydrolysis (Liu et al., 2017; Johnson and Chen, 2018; Kim and Chen, 2018; Olsen et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2017, Johnson and Chen, 2018, Kim and Chen, 2018, Olsen et al., 2020, Song et al., 2021, and Huang et al., 2023.

claim: Mutant cycle analysis confirmed strong energetic coupling between positions 1371 and 576 in hCFTR/E1371Q throughout the bursting state.
source: Mutant cycle analysis indeed confirmed strong energetic coupling between positions 1371 and 576 in hCFTR/E1371Q throughout the bursting state (Figure 3A–C), maintained even during flickery closures (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-F.

claim: The energetic coupling between positions 1371 and 576 in hCFTR/E1371Q is maintained even during flickery closures.
source: Mutant cycle analysis indeed confirmed strong energetic coupling between positions 1371 and 576 in hCFTR/E1371Q throughout the bursting state (Figure 3A–C), maintained even during flickery closures (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: The distance between all other D-loop functional groups and either polar group of the hQ1371 side chain is >4.2 Å.
source: Of note, based on our functional results per se it would remain possible that hQ1371 interacts with some other NBD1 D-loop residue. However, the structure (whose resolution in this region is particularly high) does not support any alternative interaction: the distance between all other D-loop functional groups and either polar group of the hQ1371 side chain is >4.2 Å.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the structural data.

claim: Formation of the H-bond between hQ1371 and hG576 in the E-to-Q mutant seems a unique feature of hCFTR, since the analogous positions are further apart in OF structures of both zCFTR (4.3 Å) and of other ABCC proteins (e.g., 4.7 Å in bovine MRP1, PDBID: 6bhu).
source: Interestingly, formation of that H-bond in the E-to-Q mutant seems a unique feature of hCFTR, since the analogous positions are further apart in OF structures of both zCFTR (4.3 Å) and of other ABCC proteins (e.g., 4.7 Å in bovine MRP1, PDBID: 6bhu).
evidence: This is based on comparison of structural data from multiple ABC proteins.

claim: In several ABC proteins Walker A K-to-A and Walker B D-to-N mutations were shown to decrease the rate of ATP hydrolysis below the limit of detection.
source: In several ABC proteins Walker A K-to-A and Walker B D-to-N mutations were shown to decrease the rate of ATP hydrolysis below the limit of detection (Ramjeesingh et al., 1999; Urbatsch et al., 1998; Hrycyna et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramjeesingh et al., 1999, Urbatsch et al., 1998, and Hrycyna et al., 1999.

claim: For hCFTR ATPase activity of the Walker B mutant D1370N has not been directly measured.
source: However, the sensitivities of such enzymatic assays are limited, and for hCFTR ATPase activity of the Walker B mutant D1370N has not been directly measured.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Mutation hE1371S does not significantly slow closing rate of either hK1250A or hD1370N Walker mutants.
source: We found that mutation hE1371S does not significantly slow closing rate of either Walker mutant (Figure 5B, C, Figure 5D, E), confirming that all three mutations (hK1250A, hD1370N, and hE1371S) individually abolish ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: All three mutations (hK1250A, hD1370N, and hE1371S) individually abolish ATP hydrolysis.
source: We found that mutation hE1371S does not significantly slow closing rate of either Walker mutant (Figure 5B, C, Figure 5D, E), confirming that all three mutations (hK1250A, hD1370N, and hE1371S) individually abolish ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effects.

claim: Neither hK1250A nor hE1371S mutations significantly alter the stability of the B1 state.
source: Furthermore, the mutual lack of effect of mutation hE1371S on τb of hK1250A (Figure 5B, C, blue vs. gray) and of mutation hK1250A on τb of hE1371S CFTR (Figure 5B, C, blue vs. Figure 3A, B, blue) suggests that neither of those two mutations significantly alters the stability of the B1 state.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutual lack of effect of the mutations.

claim: τb of hK1250A or hE1371S CFTR can be taken as relatively unbiased estimates of the life time of the B1 state in WT hCFTR, suggesting a true k−1 of ~0.03 s−1.
source: Thus, τb of hK1250A or hE1371S CFTR can be taken as relatively unbiased estimates of the life time of the B1 state in WT hCFTR, suggesting a true k−1 of ~0.03 s−1 (Figure 6, red).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Mutation hE1371S failed to significantly alter τb of hD1370N CFTR.
source: Consistent with that notion, mutation hE1371S also failed to significantly alter τb of another non-hydrolytic background construct, hD1370N CFTR (Figure 5D, E, blue vs. gray).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Mutation hD1370N dramatically shortened τb of both hE1371S (by ~14-fold) and hE1371Q (by ~15-fold) CFTR.
source: In contrast, mutation hD1370N dramatically shortened τb of both hE1371S (by ~14-fold, Figure 5D, E, blue vs. Figure 3A, B, blue) and hE1371Q (by ~15-fold, Figure 5D, E, black vs. Figure 3A, B, black) CFTR, suggesting that the shorter τb of the hD1370N single mutant compared to other non-hydrolytic mutants is explained by a large destabilizing effect of the hD1370N mutation on B1-state stability, as opposed to substantial residual ATP-ase activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D, 5E, and Figure 3A, 3B.

claim: The shorter τb of the hD1370N single mutant compared to other non-hydrolytic mutants is explained by a large destabilizing effect of the hD1370N mutation on B1-state stability, as opposed to substantial residual ATP-ase activity.
source: In contrast, mutation hD1370N dramatically shortened τb of both hE1371S (by ~14-fold, Figure 5D, E, blue vs. Figure 3A, B, blue) and hE1371Q (by ~15-fold, Figure 5D, E, black vs. Figure 3A, B, black) CFTR, suggesting that the shorter τb of the hD1370N single mutant compared to other non-hydrolytic mutants is explained by a large destabilizing effect of the hD1370N mutation on B1-state stability, as opposed to substantial residual ATP-ase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The monotonically decaying distribution of hD1370N burst durations is interpreted to reflect (near-) equilibrium gating of the mutant.
source: That conclusion is consistent with the monotonically decaying distribution of hD1370N burst durations, interpreted to reflect (near-) equilibrium gating of the mutant (Csanády et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Csanády et al., 2010.

claim: Mutation hE1371Q greatly increases τb when introduced into any other non-hydrolytic background: by ~13-fold in the hE1371S background, by ~16-fold in the hD1370N background, but only by ~5-fold in the hK1250A background.
source: Mutation hE1371Q indeed greatly increases τb when introduced into any other non-hydrolytic background: by ~13-fold in the hE1371S background (Figure 3A, B, black vs. blue), by ~16-fold in the hD1370N background (Figure 5D, E, black vs. gray), but only by ~5-fold in the hK1250A background (Figure 5B, C, black vs. gray).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, 3B, Figure 5D, 5E, and Figure 5B, 5C.

claim: The K1250A mutation may cause a slight increase in the hG576-hQ1371 distance, resulting in a small (~0.6 kT) but significant (p = 0.003) decrease in the strength of the non-native H-bond.
source: A possible explanation for the latter smaller effect could be that the K1250A mutation causes a slight increase in the hG576-hQ1371 distance, resulting in a small (~0.6 kT) but significant (p = 0.003) decrease in the strength of the non-native H-bond.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Non-hydrolytic τb is decreased ~5- to 10-fold by NBD1 Walker A mutation hK464A.
source: Indeed, whereas non-hydrolytic τb is decreased ~5- to 10-fold by NBD1 Walker A mutation hK464A (Powe et al., 2002; Vergani et al., 2003; Csanády et al., 2010; Csanády et al., 2013), it is increased ~3-fold by NBD2 signature sequence mutation hH1348A (Szollosi et al., 2011; Csanády et al., 2013) or by N6-(2-phenylethyl)-ATP (P-ATP) bound in site 1 (Tsai et al., 2010; Csanády et al., 2013), consistent with the notion that even site 1 undergoes substantial conformational changes coincident with pore opening/closure (Csanády et al., 2013; Mihályi et al., 2016; Sorum et al., 2017; cf., cartoon in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Powe et al., 2002, Vergani et al., 2003, Csanády et al., 2010, and Csanády et al., 2013.

claim: Non-hydrolytic τb is increased ~3-fold by NBD2 signature sequence mutation hH1348A.
source: Indeed, whereas non-hydrolytic τb is decreased ~5- to 10-fold by NBD1 Walker A mutation hK464A (Powe et al., 2002; Vergani et al., 2003; Csanády et al., 2010; Csanády et al., 2013), it is increased ~3-fold by NBD2 signature sequence mutation hH1348A (Szollosi et al., 2011; Csanády et al., 2013) or by N6-(2-phenylethyl)-ATP (P-ATP) bound in site 1 (Tsai et al., 2010; Csanády et al., 2013), consistent with the notion that even site 1 undergoes substantial conformational changes coincident with pore opening/closure (Csanády et al., 2013; Mihályi et al., 2016; Sorum et al., 2017; cf., cartoon in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Szollosi et al., 2011 and Csanády et al., 2013.

claim: Non-hydrolytic τb is increased ~3-fold by N6-(2-phenylethyl)-ATP (P-ATP) bound in site 1.
source: Indeed, whereas non-hydrolytic τb is decreased ~5- to 10-fold by NBD1 Walker A mutation hK464A (Powe et al., 2002; Vergani et al., 2003; Csanády et al., 2010; Csanády et al., 2013), it is increased ~3-fold by NBD2 signature sequence mutation hH1348A (Szollosi et al., 2011; Csanády et al., 2013) or by N6-(2-phenylethyl)-ATP (P-ATP) bound in site 1 (Tsai et al., 2010; Csanády et al., 2013), consistent with the notion that even site 1 undergoes substantial conformational changes coincident with pore opening/closure (Csanády et al., 2013; Mihályi et al., 2016; Sorum et al., 2017; cf., cartoon in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsai et al., 2010 and Csanády et al., 2013.

claim: Even site 1 undergoes substantial conformational changes coincident with pore opening/closure.
source: Indeed, whereas non-hydrolytic τb is decreased ~5- to 10-fold by NBD1 Walker A mutation hK464A (Powe et al., 2002; Vergani et al., 2003; Csanády et al., 2010; Csanády et al., 2013), it is increased ~3-fold by NBD2 signature sequence mutation hH1348A (Szollosi et al., 2011; Csanády et al., 2013) or by N6-(2-phenylethyl)-ATP (P-ATP) bound in site 1 (Tsai et al., 2010; Csanády et al., 2013), consistent with the notion that even site 1 undergoes substantial conformational changes coincident with pore opening/closure (Csanády et al., 2013; Mihályi et al., 2016; Sorum et al., 2017; cf., cartoon in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Csanády et al., 2013, Mihályi et al., 2016, and Sorum et al., 2017.

claim: Slowing of site 2 separation by the non-natural H bond prolongs bursts.
source: However, our results directly demonstrate that separation around site 2 remains the prevalent pathway for pore closure even in the absence of ATP hydrolysis. If that were not the case then slowing of site 2 separation by the non-natural H bond would not be expected to prolong bursts.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing prolonged bursts in E1371Q.

claim: Separation around site 2 remains the prevalent pathway for pore closure even in the absence of ATP hydrolysis.
source: However, our results directly demonstrate that separation around site 2 remains the prevalent pathway for pore closure even in the absence of ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: If in hE1371S or hD1370N channels pore closure predominantly proceeded through dissociation of site 1 then further stabilization of site 2 by introduction of the E1371Q mutation would not be expected to prolong τb.
source: Specifically, if in hE1371S or hD1370N channels pore closure predominantly proceeded through dissociation of site 1 then further stabilization of site 2 by introduction of the E1371Q mutation would not be expected to prolong τb – in contrast to the ~13- to 16-fold prolongation observed in both backgrounds (Figure 3A, B, black vs. blue; Figure 5D, E, black vs. gray).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the kinetic model.

claim: The lack of effect on k−1 of mutations hK1250A and hE1371S is in line with the suggestion that inter-NBD contacts are already established in T‡.
source: The lack of effect on k−1 of mutations hK1250A and hE1371S demonstrated here is in line with that suggestion.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The ~15-fold increase and decrease in non-hydrolytic τb caused by mutations hE1371Q and hD1370N, respectively, indicate that those two side chains undergo significant rearrangements even during the T‡ ↔ B1 gating step.
source: On the other hand, the ~15-fold increase and decrease in non-hydrolytic τb caused by mutations hE1371Q and hD1370N, respectively, clearly indicate that those two side chains (located near the center of the NBD dimer interface between sites 1 and 2; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) undergo significant rearrangements even during the T‡ ↔ B1 gating step.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: In hCFTR's NBD2 subdomain closure is fully completed only in the NBD-dimerized state.
source: Comparison of all three structures shows that in hCFTR's NBD2 that 'subdomain closure' is fully completed only in the NBD-dimerized state (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), reminiscent to earlier findings on the maltose transporter (Orelle et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and citation to Orelle et al., 2010.

claim: Subdomain closure strengthens multiple interactions of the hD1370 side-chain carboxylate, by reducing its distance both to the Mg2+ ion (from ~5.0 to 3.7 Å) and to the hS1251 side chain (from ~4.1 to 3.0 Å).
source: That movement strengthens multiple interactions of the hD1370 side-chain carboxylate, by reducing its distance both to the Mg2+ ion (from ~5.0 to 3.7 Å) and to the hS1251 side chain (from ~4.1 to 3.0 Å) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: If subdomain closure happens during step T‡ ↔ B1 then lack of tightening interactions in hD1370N could explain selective destabilization of the B1 state relative to T‡ in the mutant.
source: If that movement happened during step T‡ ↔ B1 then lack of those tightening interactions in hD1370N could explain selective destabilization of the B1 state relative to T‡ in the mutant.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Assuming k−1 < 0.2 s−1 and k1 ~ 4 s−1, a lower limit of ~0.95 was provided for the CR of prephosphorylated WT hCFTR gating at 25°C.
source: In the past, assuming k−1 < 0.2 s−1 and k1 ~ 4 s−1, a lower limit of ~0.95 was provided for the CR of prephosphorylated WT hCFTR gating at 25°C (Csanády et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Csanády et al., 2010.

claim: The present estimate of k−1 ~ 0.03 s−1 under the same conditions provides a more accurate value of CR ~0.99.
source: Our present estimate of k−1 ~ 0.03 s−1 under the same conditions provides a more accurate value of CR ~0.99.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data.

claim: Only 1 out of a ~100 bursts is terminated by non-hydrolytic separation of site 2.
source: Thus, only 1 out of a ~100 bursts is terminated by non-hydrolytic separation of site 2 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is calculated from the coupling ratio.

claim: Based on the measured activation enthalpies (ΔH‡B1→B2 ~ 70 kJ/mol, ΔH‡B1→IB1 ~ 40 kJ/mol), k1 is ~3-fold faster (~12 s−1) and k−1 ~ 1.9-fold faster (~0.06 s−1) at 37°C.
source: Based on the measured activation enthalpies (ΔH‡B1→B2 ~ 70 kJ/mol, ΔH‡B1→IB1 ~ 40 kJ/mol; Csanády et al., 2006), k1 is ~3-fold faster (~12 s−1) and k−1 ~ 1.9-fold faster (~0.06 s−1) at 37°C, predicting a CR of ~0.995.
evidence: This is calculated from the activation enthalpies reported in Csanády et al., 2006.

claim: At 37°C the predicted CR is ~0.995.
source: Based on the measured activation enthalpies (ΔH‡B1→B2 ~ 70 kJ/mol, ΔH‡B1→IB1 ~ 40 kJ/mol; Csanády et al., 2006), k1 is ~3-fold faster (~12 s−1) and k−1 ~ 1.9-fold faster (~0.06 s−1) at 37°C, predicting a CR of ~0.995.
evidence: This is calculated from the temperature-adjusted rate constants.

claim: The presence of PKA slows both k1 and k−1 rates by ~twofold.
source: On the other hand, the presence of PKA slows both rates by ~twofold (Csanády et al., 2010; Vergani et al., 2003), predicting little effect on the CR.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Csanády et al., 2010 and Vergani et al., 2003.

claim: The presence of PKA has little effect on the CR.
source: On the other hand, the presence of PKA slows both rates by ~twofold (Csanády et al., 2010; Vergani et al., 2003), predicting little effect on the CR.
evidence: This is inferred from the proportional slowing of both rates.

claim: A strong native H-bond between extracellular loops 1 and 6 of hCFTR (between residues R117 and E1124) was shown to be present only in the open state, but disrupted during both IB and flickery closures.
source: A strong native H-bond between extracellular loops 1 and 6 of hCFTR (between residues R117 and E1124) was shown to be present only in the open state, but disrupted during both IB and flickery closures (Simon and Csanády, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Simon and Csanády, 2021.

claim: The non-native hQ1371–hG576 H-bond is maintained during flickery closures, and disrupted only during IB closures.
source: In contrast, we show here that the non-native hQ1371–hG576 H-bond is maintained during flickery closures, and disrupted only during IB closures (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Flickery closures of hE1371Q CFTR involve local movements confined to the external ends of the TMD helices but no disruption of the tight NBD dimer.
source: These findings are consistent with the notion that flickery closures of hE1371Q CFTR involve local movements confined to the external ends of the TMD helices but no disruption of the tight NBD dimer, whereas IB closures represent a global rearrangement during which site 2 of the NBD dimer opens up to allow nucleotide exchange.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: IB closures represent a global rearrangement during which site 2 of the NBD dimer opens up to allow nucleotide exchange.
source: These findings are consistent with the notion that flickery closures of hE1371Q CFTR involve local movements confined to the external ends of the TMD helices but no disruption of the tight NBD dimer, whereas IB closures represent a global rearrangement during which site 2 of the NBD dimer opens up to allow nucleotide exchange.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The extent of NBD separation during IB closures is large enough to disrupt the site 2 interfacial H-bonds formed between the side chains of hT1246 and hR555 in WT (or K1250R) hCFTR and between residues hQ1371 and hG576 in E1371Q hCFTR.
source: The precise extent of that separation is presently unknown: it is large enough to disrupt the site 2 interfacial H-bonds (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) formed between the side chains of hT1246 and hR555 in WT (or K1250R) hCFTR (Vergani et al., 2005) and between residues hQ1371 and hG576 in E1371Q hCFTR (Figures 2E and 3A–C), but too small to be detected by a pair of FRET sensors engineered into position h388 of NBD1 and position h1435 of NBD2 (Levring et al., 2023).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and citations.

claim: The extent of NBD separation during IB closures is too small to be detected by a pair of FRET sensors engineered into position h388 of NBD1 and position h1435 of NBD2.
source: The precise extent of that separation is presently unknown: it is large enough to disrupt the site 2 interfacial H-bonds (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) formed between the side chains of hT1246 and hR555 in WT (or K1250R) hCFTR (Vergani et al., 2005) and between residues hQ1371 and hG576 in E1371Q hCFTR (Figures 2E and 3A–C), but too small to be detected by a pair of FRET sensors engineered into position h388 of NBD1 and position h1435 of NBD2 (Levring et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Levring et al., 2023.

claim: Precisely gauging the extent of NBD motions during IB closures will require a cryo-EM structure of the active IB state of phosphorylated hCFTR in the presence of ATP.
source: Precisely gauging the extent of those motions will require a cryo-EM structure of the active IB state of phosphorylated hCFTR in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is stated as a future direction.
